rationales: Advanced strategies often help but are not guaranteed to win on every corpus.
Small chunks favour precise facts but can lose context; it depends on the questions.
Correct. A side-by-side evaluation on representative questions is the defensible method.
An LLM's preference is not evidence of retrieval performance on your data.

sources.title: Evaluate and monitor — MLflow 3 GenAI on Databricks

questions.scenario: Chunks from long technical manuals often start or end mid-thought, and retrieved chunks lack the context needed to interpret them.
questions.stem: Which two practices reduce this loss of context? (Select two.)
options: Add a modest overlap between neighbouring chunks.
Prepend the document title and section heading to each chunk.
Lowercase the text and remove stopwords before embedding.
Split strictly every N characters regardless of sentence boundaries.
questions.explanation: Overlap keeps boundary-straddling sentences whole in at least one chunk, and contextual headers tell the embedding and the LLM where a chunk sits in the document. Removing stopwords harms dense embeddings trained on natural text, and hard character splits cause the problem.
rationales: Correct. Overlap protects content that crosses chunk boundaries.
Correct. Title and heading context make each chunk interpretable on its own.
Dense embedding models expect natural text; this degrades meaning rather than adding context.
Splitting without regard to sentences is what creates mid-thought chunks.

questions.scenario: A team is starting a new tool-calling agent on Databricks. They want to write it in LangGraph, try it on their laptops, and then deploy it with tracing enabled, following the current recommended path.
questions.stem: Which approach fits best?
options: Write a notebook that pickles the LangGraph object and uploads it to a UC volume for an app to load at start-up
Create a Model Serving endpoint first, then write a class with predict() and edit it in place on the endpoint
Scaffold with agentbricks init using the langgraph template, run it with agentbricks dev, and deploy with agentbricks deploy
Build the agent in AI Playground and export it as the production artifact
questions.explanation: The Agent Bricks CLI is the current code-first path: init scaffolds from a langgraph template, dev runs locally and deploy publishes to Agent Runtime with MLflow tracing on by default. Model Serving agents and AI Playground are in the legacy section.
rationales: Pickling to a volume skips deployment, tracing and governance; it is not a documented deployment path.
Agents on Model Serving are now legacy, and endpoints are not edited in place.
Correct. This is the documented init/dev/deploy flow with a LangGraph template.
AI Playground is legacy and is for trying models, not producing deployable agents.

questions.scenario: A team already has a working agent written with the OpenAI Agents SDK. They want to move it onto the Agent Bricks CLI workflow without rewriting it from scratch.
questions.stem: What should they do?
options: Use the Agent Bricks CLI init with its --existing option to migrate the current agent
Rewrite the agent in LangGraph, because the CLI only accepts LangGraph projects
Wrap the agent in a SQL UDF and call it from a dashboard
Register the agent as a Genie Agent so the CLI can discover it
questions.explanation: The CLI supports migrating an existing agent with --existing, and it also has an openai template for the OpenAI Agents SDK. A rewrite is unnecessary.
rationales: Correct. --existing is the documented way to bring an existing agent into a CLI project.
The CLI also has an openai template; LangGraph is not required.
A SQL UDF is not a way to host or migrate an agent.
Genie Agents are NL-to-SQL chats, not a container for custom agent code.

questions.scenario: An agent built with the Agent Bricks CLI calls a tool that writes audit records to a table. Business users who chat with the agent do not have, and should not get, write access to that table. The security team accepts that this one tool runs under a dedicated identity.
questions.stem: How should the tool be configured?
options: Grant every business user MODIFY on the audit table so the default identity works
Store a personal access token for an admin in the agent code
Leave the default; tools always run as a shared workspace identity
Run the tool as the app service principal using the --auth app option and grant that principal access
questions.explanation: By default CLI tools run as the requesting user, which would fail here. The --auth app option runs them as the app service principal, which can be granted exactly the access the tool needs.
rationales: This widens access for every user, which the requirement forbids.
Hard-coding an admin token is a security anti-pattern and gives far too much access.
The default is the requesting user, not a shared identity.
Correct. --auth app switches the tool identity to the app service principal.

questions.scenario: A prompt template is stored in the MLflow Prompt Registry with variables written as {{question}} and {{context}}. A developer loads it and passes the template string directly into a LangChain prompt template, and the variables are not filled in.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Re-register the prompt with no variables and concatenate strings in code
Call to_single_brace_format() on the loaded prompt before passing it to LangChain
Move the prompt to a UC volume as a text file
Switch the alias to an older version of the prompt
questions.explanation: Prompt Registry templates use double braces, while LangChain uses single braces. The registry provides to_single_brace_format() for exactly this case.
rationales: Dropping variables loses the benefit of templating and versioning.
Correct. This converts {{var}} to the single-brace format LangChain expects.
Storing a text file in a volume loses versioning and does not fix the format.
Every version uses the same double-brace syntax, so changing alias does not help.

questions.scenario: A policy Q&A assistant built on retrieval sometimes invents policy details that do not appear in any document. The team wants to change the prompt to reduce this.
questions.stem: Which two prompt changes help most? (Select two.)
options: Insert the retrieved passages with a source id for each and ask the model to cite them
Raise the temperature so the model explores more possible answers
Instruct the model to answer only from the provided passages and to say it does not know when they do not contain the answer
Remove the system prompt so the model is less constrained
questions.explanation: Grounding the answer in labelled passages and giving an explicit rule for missing information both reduce invented content. Higher temperature and fewer instructions push the other way.
rationales: Correct. Labelled context gives the model grounded material and makes answers checkable.
Higher temperature increases randomness, which tends to increase invented details.
Correct. An explicit fallback stops the model guessing when context is missing.
Removing instructions removes the guardrail that keeps answers grounded.

questions.scenario: A downstream service parses the model output as JSON. About one answer in ten comes back as prose or with extra text around the JSON.
questions.stem: What should the team try first?
options: Fine-tune a new model on a few thousand JSON examples
Switch to the largest available model and change nothing else
Lower max tokens so long prose answers are cut off
Add an explicit output-format instruction with one example of the exact JSON, then re-run the evaluation set
questions.explanation: A clear format instruction plus a worked example is the cheapest, most direct prompt adjustment for format problems, and re-running the evaluation set shows whether it worked. Fine-tuning or a model swap is premature.
rationales: Fine-tuning is costly and slow; try prompt adjustment first.
A bigger model may not fix format adherence and adds cost without measurement.
Truncation produces broken JSON rather than valid JSON.
Correct. Targeted prompt adjustment, then measure.

sources.title: Evaluate and monitor — MLflow 3 GenAI docs

questions.scenario: An engineer rewrites a RAG system prompt. After reading four answers that look better, they want to make the new version the default for all users.
questions.stem: What is the best next step?
options: Run the old and new prompt versions over the same evaluation dataset with the same scorers using mlflow.genai.evaluate() and compare
Ship it now and roll back if users complain
Ask the model which prompt it prefers
Read four more answers from the new prompt only
questions.explanation: A fair comparison needs both versions scored on the same dataset with the same scorers. A handful of hand-picked outputs is not evidence and can hide regressions.
rationales: Correct. This is controlled evaluation of a prompt change.
Using users as the test set risks a visible regression.
Asking the model for its preference is not a measurement of answer quality.
More samples from one version still give no comparison.

sources.title: Evaluate and monitor — MLflow 3 GenAI docs

questions.scenario: A company must stop US Social Security numbers from being sent to a model endpoint, including inside MCP tool calls that its agents make.
questions.stem: Which control fits best?
options: A sentence in the system prompt telling the model to ignore SSNs
A production monitoring scorer that flags SSNs after the response
A Unity Gateway service policy using the built-in Sensitive Data Detection policy at the input phase
An AI Search filter on the retrieval index
questions.explanation: Sensitive Data Detection is a built-in service policy that can block PII such as SSNs, including in MCP tool calls, and the input phase acts before the model receives the request.
rationales: The SSN still reaches the model, and prompt rules can be bypassed.
Monitoring scores traces after the fact; it does not stop the data being sent.
Correct. A gateway policy enforces the block outside the model.
A retrieval filter does not inspect user requests or tool calls.

sources.title: Moderate model traffic — Unity Gateway docs

questions.scenario: A team wants to check every model response for unsafe content and stop it before it reaches the user, regardless of what the prompt says.
questions.stem: Where should this check run?
options: In a nightly job over the inference table
At the input phase, before the request reaches the model
In a production monitoring scorer with a 100% sample rate
At the output phase of a Unity Gateway service policy
questions.explanation: Output-phase policies run after the model generates a response and before it is returned, so they can stop it. Input-phase policies only see the request; monitoring and nightly jobs act too late.
rationales: A nightly job finds problems after users have seen them.
The input phase sees the request, not the generated response.
Monitoring scores traces but does not block responses.
Correct. The output phase screens the response before it is returned.

questions.scenario: A team deployed a custom agent as a custom model on a serving endpoint and turned on the legacy AI Gateway guardrails, expecting PII in responses to be masked. Testing shows PII still appears.
questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Masking needs a Genie Agent in front of the endpoint
PII masking only runs when temperature is zero
Guardrails apply only to requests sent through SQL
Legacy AI Gateway guardrails are not supported on custom model endpoints
questions.explanation: The legacy AI Gateway guardrails do not support custom model endpoints, and even where supported, detection is not guaranteed complete. A different control, such as a Unity Gateway service policy, is needed.
rationales: Genie Agents are NL-to-SQL chats and play no part in PII masking.
Temperature has nothing to do with guardrail support.
No such restriction exists; the issue is endpoint type.
Correct. Custom model endpoints are excluded from legacy guardrails.

sources.title: Configure AI Gateway on endpoints — Databricks docs

questions.scenario: A data engineer runs a large batch classification job with ai_query against a system.ai model and assumes the same controls apply as for the interactive endpoints.
questions.stem: Which two controls do apply to these calls? (Select two.)
options: Gateway guardrails
Usage tracking
Inference table logging
Permission checks
questions.explanation: ai_query calls to system.ai route through Unity Gateway, which applies usage tracking, budgets and permission checks. Guardrails, inference tables, rate limits and fallbacks do not apply.
rationales: Guardrails are explicitly not applied to these calls.
Correct. Usage is tracked.
Inference tables do not apply to ai_query.
Correct. Permission checks apply.

questions.scenario: A support assistant must follow house rules: never promise a refund, always offer a human hand-off, and keep a formal tone. There are no reference answers.
questions.stem: Which MLflow judge is the best fit for checking these rules?
options: Correctness
RetrievalSufficiency
Guidelines
ToolCallCorrectness
questions.explanation: The Guidelines judge checks responses against plain-language rules and needs no ground truth. The other three need expected answers or expected tool calls.
rationales: Correctness compares against an expected answer, which does not exist here.
RetrievalSufficiency needs ground truth and judges retrieval, not tone.
Correct. Guidelines checks custom natural-language rules.
ToolCallCorrectness needs ground truth and judges tool calls, not tone.

questions.scenario: Before launch, a team wants a quick read on whether any answers from its assistant contain harmful content. They have a set of realistic user questions but no labelled answers.
questions.stem: Which judge should they run?
options: ToolCallCorrectness
Correctness
RetrievalSufficiency
Safety
questions.explanation: The Safety judge assesses harmful content and does not need ground truth, so it works with unlabelled questions.
rationales: ToolCallCorrectness requires expected tool calls.
Correctness requires expected answers.
RetrievalSufficiency requires ground truth and measures retrieval coverage.
Correct. Safety needs no labelled answers.

questions.scenario: A team is assembling an offline evaluation dataset and must decide which judges will need an expected answer or expected facts in each row.
questions.stem: Which two built-in judges require ground truth? (Select two.)
options: Correctness
Safety
RelevanceToQuery
RetrievalSufficiency
questions.explanation: Correctness, RetrievalSufficiency and ToolCallCorrectness need ground truth. Safety and RelevanceToQuery work without it.
rationales: Correct. It compares against an expected answer.
Safety needs no ground truth.
RelevanceToQuery needs no ground truth.
Correct. It checks whether retrieval covered the expected facts.

questions.scenario: A healthcare company needs predictable performance for a production LLM workload and must meet HIPAA requirements.
questions.stem: Which Foundation Model APIs mode fits best?
options: Standard pay-per-token
AI Playground
Provisioned throughput
Priority pay-per-token on every request
questions.explanation: Provisioned throughput is the documented choice for performance guarantees and HIPAA workloads, and it can be on-demand or reserved.
rationales: Shared pay-per-token capacity does not give performance guarantees.
AI Playground is a legacy testing UI, not a serving mode.
Correct. Performance guarantees and HIPAA point to provisioned throughput.
Priority pay-per-token raises priority per request but is not the documented answer for guarantees and HIPAA.

questions.scenario: A team has fine-tuned an open model for its domain and needs to serve it for a production application.
questions.stem: Which serving mode should they plan for?
options: Pay-per-token on the shared foundation model endpoints
Calling the base model with a longer prompt instead
Provisioned throughput
A Genie Agent
questions.explanation: Fine-tuned models are one of the documented reasons to choose provisioned throughput. Shared pay-per-token endpoints serve the Databricks-hosted base models.
rationales: Shared pay-per-token endpoints host the platform models, not your fine-tuned weights.
This abandons the fine-tuned model rather than serving it.
Correct. Provisioned throughput serves fine-tuned models.
Genie Agents answer data questions; they do not serve custom models.

questions.scenario: An app uses pay-per-token for most traffic. A small set of executive-facing requests must be served with higher priority, but the team does not want to commit to dedicated capacity.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Buy a 3-month reserved provisioned throughput term for all traffic
Retry executive requests in a tight loop until they succeed
Use priority pay-per-token by setting service_tier on just those requests
Route executive requests through ai_query batch jobs
questions.explanation: Priority pay-per-token is selected per request with service_tier, so only the important requests pay for priority and no capacity commitment is needed.
rationales: A reserved term commits to dedicated capacity, which the team wants to avoid.
Tight retry loops add load and are an anti-pattern.
Correct. Per-request priority matches the need.
Batch jobs suit large offline workloads, not interactive priority requests.

questions.scenario: A team must summarise several million support tickets stored in a Delta table once a quarter. A developer proposes a Python loop that calls a chat endpoint one ticket at a time.
questions.stem: What is the better approach?
options: Run the loop on a larger driver node
Paste tickets into a chat UI in batches of 100
Run the Python loop with more threads against the same endpoint
Use the ai_query AI Function over the table, preferring a batch-optimized system.ai model and submitting the full dataset in one query
questions.explanation: AI Functions are the documented batch mode. The ai_query guidance is to prefer system.ai batch-optimized models and submit the full dataset in one query rather than calling per row from client code.
rationales: A bigger driver does not change the one-at-a-time pattern.
Manual copy and paste does not scale and is not governed.
More threads still hammer an interactive endpoint and add failure handling work.
Correct. ai_query is designed for batch inference over tables.

questions.scenario: A RAG app sends a long system prompt, the top 20 retrieved chunks and the full chat history on every turn. Long conversations start failing with context-length errors.
questions.stem: Which change addresses the root cause with the least side effect on answer quality?
options: Switch to a smaller embedding model
Remove the system prompt entirely
Increase max output tokens
Reduce the number of chunks based on evaluation results and summarise older chat history
questions.explanation: Everything in the request must fit the LLM context window. Tuning chunk count with evaluation and summarising history cuts input size while keeping the relevant material.
rationales: The embedding model does not change how much text the LLM receives.
Removing instructions hurts behaviour and only saves a small part of the input.
More output tokens use more of the window and make the problem worse.
Correct. It shrinks the input while keeping what matters.

questions.scenario: A team switched its document index to a newer embedding model and re-embedded all documents. Retrieval quality then dropped sharply. Investigation shows the application still embeds user queries with the previous model.
questions.stem: What is the problem?
options: The new model has a higher vector dimension, which AI Search does not support
The index needs a re-ranker to compensate for the change
Hybrid search must be turned off after any model change
Queries and documents must be embedded with the same model; vectors from different models are not comparable
questions.explanation: Similarity search compares a query vector with document vectors, which only works when both come from the same embedding model. Mixing models produces meaningless similarity scores.
rationales: Dimension is not the cause described, and AI Search supports large dimensions.
A re-ranker cannot fix candidates retrieved with incompatible vectors.
Hybrid search is a recommended starting point; it is not the issue.
Correct. Embed queries and documents with one model.

questions.scenario: A team wants to attach an existing AI Search index to a Knowledge Assistant (legacy). The index was built with a self-hosted embedding model that is not served by Databricks.
questions.stem: What should they expect?
options: Any index works as long as it has a text column
The assistant will re-embed the index automatically with its own model
It is not supported; an attached index must use databricks-gte-large-en, databricks-bge-large-en or databricks-qwen3-embedding-0-6b
It works only if the index is a Direct Vector Access index
questions.explanation: The Knowledge Assistant documentation limits attached AI Search indexes to three Databricks embedding models. An index built with another model has to be rebuilt.
rationales: The documented requirement is about the embedding model, not just a text column.
There is no documented automatic re-embedding.
Correct. Only the listed embedding models are accepted.
Index type does not lift the embedding model requirement.

questions.scenario: Three candidate LLMs were evaluated on the same dataset with the same scorers. Model A scores highest on quality but its median latency is three times the product's latency budget. Model B scores slightly lower, meets the budget and costs less per request. Model C meets the budget but fails the minimum quality bar.
questions.stem: Which model should the team choose?
options: Model A, because quality always comes first
Model C, because it is the cheapest that meets latency
None; evaluate again with a different dataset for each model
Model B, because it meets every hard constraint with the best quality among those that do
questions.explanation: The right pick is the best model that satisfies all hard constraints. A breaks the latency budget and C misses the quality bar, so B wins.
rationales: A fails a hard latency constraint.
C fails the minimum quality bar.
Using different datasets per model would make the comparison unfair.
Correct. B is the best model within all constraints.

sources.title: Evaluate and monitor — MLflow 3 GenAI docs

questions.scenario: An agent sometimes calls the wrong tool for a request, and the final answer is then wrong. The team wants to see exactly where the reasoning went off course.
questions.stem: What should they look at first?
options: The model card of the LLM
The serving endpoint CPU metrics
The Delta table history of the source data
The MLflow trace for a failing request, which records intermediate steps such as tool calls with their inputs and outputs
questions.explanation: MLflow traces capture inputs, outputs and intermediate steps, including tool calls, so they show where an agent made the wrong choice.
rationales: A model card describes the model in general, not a specific failing run.
Infrastructure metrics do not show which tool was chosen or why.
Data history does not show agent decisions.
Correct. Traces show each step of the agent run.

questions.scenario: A team asks how offline evaluation and production monitoring differ in the GenAI lifecycle on Databricks.
questions.stem: Which statement is accurate?
options: They are the same process run on different clusters
Evaluation can only use code scorers, while monitoring can only use LLM judges
Monitoring blocks unsafe responses in real time, while evaluation only produces reports
Evaluation runs mlflow.genai.evaluate() on a fixed dataset before deployment; monitoring runs registered scorers on sampled live traces after deployment
questions.explanation: Evaluation compares versions on a fixed dataset before shipping. Monitoring continuously scores a sample of production traces. Neither blocks responses; that is the job of guardrails.
rationales: They have different inputs and purposes.
Both stages can use judges and code scorers.
Monitoring observes and scores; it does not block responses.
Correct. This is the documented split.

sources.title: Evaluate and monitor — MLflow 3 GenAI docs

questions.scenario: A team wants to monitor a production assistant. A draft plan schedules the Correctness judge on 100% of live traffic.
questions.stem: What is the main problem with this plan?
options: Correctness only works on multi-turn sessions
Monitoring cannot use any built-in judges
Live traffic has no expected answers, so a ground-truth judge like Correctness is unsuitable; use judges such as Safety, Guidelines or RelevanceToQuery
Correctness must be registered in a separate workspace
questions.explanation: Correctness needs ground truth, which production requests do not carry. Judges that need no ground truth are the right choice for monitoring, ideally at a sample rate that controls cost.
rationales: Correctness is a single-turn judge; session judges are separate.
Built-in judges such as Safety can be registered for monitoring.
Correct. Choose judges that need no ground truth for live traffic.
There is no such requirement.

questions.scenario: A team is setting up production monitoring (Beta) for an agent experiment.
questions.stem: Which two statements are accurate? (Select two.)
options: An experiment can have up to 20 active scorers
Every scorer must score 100% of traces
Monitoring results typically appear about 15–20 minutes after the traces
Monitoring scorers stop a bad response before it reaches the user
questions.explanation: The documented limit is 20 active scorers per experiment, and results take 15–20 minutes. Sampling rates are configurable, and monitoring observes rather than blocks.
rationales: Correct. This is the documented limit.
sample_rate is configurable, and lower rates are advised for costly judges.
Correct. Results are not instant.
Monitoring runs after the fact; blocking is a guardrail job.

questions.scenario: A team writes custom Python logic that checks whether an answer includes a valid ticket number, and wants it to run as part of production monitoring.
questions.stem: How should the custom scorer be written?
options: As a SQL view over the inference table
As a Genie Agent instruction
As a guardrail service policy
As a function decorated with @scorer
questions.explanation: Custom code scorers are written with @scorer, and production monitoring requires custom scorers to use only @scorer.
rationales: A SQL view is not a monitoring scorer.
Genie instructions guide SQL generation, not scoring.
A service policy enforces input or output rules; it does not record quality assessments on traces.
Correct. @scorer is the supported form.

questions.scenario: A developer inherits an agent that runs on Databricks Apps. Its code has module-level functions decorated with @invoke() and @stream(), and clients call it at a /responses path.
questions.stem: What is this agent built on?
options: The Supervisor Agent UI
A Genie Agent with MCP connectors
A class-based ResponsesAgent on Model Serving
The legacy MLflow AgentServer, which serves the OpenAI Responses API
questions.explanation: The MLflow AgentServer on Apps uses module-level @invoke() and @stream() functions and serves the Responses API at /responses. It is now in the legacy section, and the CLI with DurableAgentServer is the replacement.
rationales: The Supervisor Agent is configured in a UI, not with these decorators.
Genie Agents are not authored with Python decorators.
ResponsesAgent on Model Serving is class-based with predict() and predict_stream().
Correct. These are the AgentServer markers.

sources.title: Migrate an agent to Apps — Agent Framework docs

questions.scenario: An analytics team wants to call a deployed agent from existing data pipelines and from an application.
questions.stem: Which two are documented ways to query a deployed agent? (Select two.)
options: Reading the agent's Python file from a UC volume
The Responses API
SQL
Opening the MLflow experiment page
questions.explanation: Deployed agents can be queried through the invocation API, the Responses API or SQL. Reading source files or experiment pages does not execute the agent.
rationales: Reading source code does not run the deployed agent.
Correct. The Responses API is supported.
Correct. SQL is supported, which suits pipelines.
The experiment page shows runs and traces; it does not query the agent.

questions.scenario: An application calls a Genie Agent through the Genie Conversation API. Users ask "What were sales last quarter?" and then "And by region?", but the second answer ignores the first question.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Add the word "region" to every table name
Raise the agent's conversation limit
Switch from agent mode to a SQL warehouse query
Send the follow-up with the same conversation_id
questions.explanation: Follow-ups should reuse the conversation_id so Genie keeps the earlier context. Starting a new conversation loses it.
rationales: Renaming tables does not give Genie the earlier question.
The conversation limit is about volume, not context carry-over.
Bypassing Genie loses the natural-language interface and still has no context.
Correct. conversation_id ties the turns together.

questions.scenario: A team is building a code-first agent that should answer sales questions from Unity Catalog tables by delegating to an existing Genie Agent, and policy questions with a document retriever.
questions.stem: How should the Genie Agent be connected as a subagent?
options: Export Genie's generated SQL once and hard-code the queries in the agent
Copy the Genie tables into a vector index and drop Genie
Use the Genie Agent as a subagent through the built-in Databricks MCP server
Give the agent a personal access token for the person who created the Genie Agent
questions.explanation: The docs describe Genie Agents acting as subagents through the built-in Databricks MCP server. A custom orchestrator on Apps is only needed for routing that the built-in options cannot express.
rationales: Hard-coded SQL cannot answer new questions.
A vector index is for semantic retrieval, not accurate aggregate SQL answers.
Correct. This is the documented integration.
Sharing one person's token breaks per-user access control.

questions.scenario: A Supervisor Agent (exam guide: Multiagent Supervisor) coordinates a Genie Agent and an agent endpoint. Some end users get permission errors while others do not.
questions.stem: What do end users need for the supervisor's built-in access control to let them through?
options: CAN MANAGE on the supervisor only
Workspace admin rights
Nothing; the supervisor always runs as its creator
CAN QUERY on the endpoints and SELECT on the underlying tables
questions.explanation: The Supervisor Agent enforces access per user: end users need CAN QUERY on the endpoints it calls and SELECT on the tables involved.
rationales: Management rights on the supervisor do not grant access to the subagents' data.
Admin rights are far broader than needed.
Built-in access control checks the end user, not the creator.
Correct. These are the documented permissions.

questions.scenario: An analytics group wants one Genie Agent over about 120 tables covering finance, HR, supply chain and marketing.
questions.stem: What is the best design?
options: Replace Genie with a document retriever over table descriptions
Put all 120 tables in one Genie Agent and add more instructions
Create one view that joins all 120 tables
Split the data into focused Genie Agents by subject area, each within the per-agent table limit, and route between them in a multi-agent system
questions.explanation: A Genie Agent supports up to 50 tables, views or metric views, and focused agents produce more reliable SQL. Routing between subject-area agents covers the full scope.
rationales: A retriever over descriptions cannot compute aggregate answers.
120 tables exceed the per-agent limit.
A giant join view is hard to maintain and still confuses SQL generation.
Correct. This respects the limit and keeps each agent focused.

questions.scenario: A team configures a Supervisor Agent (legacy) and tries to add a Direct Vector Access index in AI Search as a retrieval subagent.
questions.stem: What should they expect?
options: It works, because any AI Search index type is accepted
It works only for up to 5 subagents
It works only after converting the index to self-managed embeddings
It is not supported; AI Search subagents must be Delta Sync indexes
questions.explanation: The Supervisor Agent documentation requires AI Search subagents to be Delta Sync indexes. The subagent limit is 50, not 5.
rationales: Index type is restricted.
The documented limit is 50 subagents.
Self-managed embeddings do not change the index type requirement.
Correct. Delta Sync is required.

questions.scenario: A team needs an assistant that answers questions in a single fixed pattern: retrieve passages, fill a template, call the model once, return the answer with citations. There are no tools and no branching.
questions.stem: Which design is most appropriate?
options: A multi-agent system with a supervisor and three subagents
An autonomous agent loop that decides whether to retrieve
A simple chain with a fixed sequence of steps
A Genie Agent over the document volume
questions.explanation: When the steps are fixed and known in advance, a chain is simpler, cheaper and easier to test than an agent loop or a multi-agent system.
rationales: Multi-agent systems add routing cost and complexity with no benefit here.
An agent loop adds latency and unpredictability for a fixed flow.
Correct. A chain matches a fixed sequence.
Genie Agents generate SQL over tables; this is a document Q&A flow.

questions.scenario: A team wraps its RAG chain in an mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel. Load tests on the serving endpoint show each request spends about 800 ms building an AI Search client and reading a 40 MB prompt-config artifact before retrieval starts.
questions.stem: What change best reduces per-request latency?
options: Increase the endpoint workload size so predict() runs on larger instances
Switch the model to provisioned throughput so set-up time is reserved capacity
Cache the client in a module-level global that predict() rebuilds when it is None on each call
Move client creation and artifact loading into load_context() and keep only per-request logic in predict()
questions.explanation: load_context() runs once when the model is loaded, while predict() runs on every request. Expensive set-up such as clients and artifacts belongs in load_context(). Bigger instances or a different billing mode do not remove work that is repeated on every request.
rationales: More compute does not stop the set-up from repeating on each call.
Provisioned throughput is a Foundation Model API mode and does not change custom pyfunc start-up logic.
As described, it still checks and may rebuild on calls. load_context() is the supported hook for one-time set-up.
Correct: one-time set-up moves out of the request path.

questions.scenario: A custom pyfunc chain runs perfectly in the notebook where it was developed. After it is registered and deployed, the serving endpoint fails to start with ModuleNotFoundError for a local package named rag_utils.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Register the model to the workspace registry instead of Unity Catalog
Add rag_utils to the input_example so MLflow detects it
Grant the endpoint CAN MANAGE on the registered model
Pass the local package with code_paths (and pin libraries in pip_requirements) when logging the model
questions.explanation: The serving container only has what was logged with the model. Local helper modules must be shipped with code_paths, and library versions pinned with pip_requirements or conda_env. The registry location, input example and permissions do not package code.
rationales: The registry location does not change which code is packaged.
input_example documents a request and does not bundle code.
Permissions do not fix a missing module.
Correct: code_paths ships local modules with the model.

questions.scenario: An engineer logs a LangChain-based RAG chain and tries to register it as prod.genai.faq_bot. Registration is rejected. The log_model call passed the chain object and pip_requirements only.
questions.stem: What should the engineer add so the model can be registered on Databricks?
options: A Champion alias set before registration
A provisioned throughput endpoint name
An input_example (or an explicit signature) so the model has a signature
A two-level model name such as genai.faq_bot
questions.explanation: Databricks requires a signature on registered models and rejects models without one. Providing an input_example lets MLflow infer the signature, or you can pass signature= explicitly. UC model names are three-level, and aliases are set after a version exists.
rationales: Aliases point at versions that already exist. They are not a registration prerequisite.
Endpoint configuration is unrelated to registering a model.
Correct: a signature is required, and an input_example lets MLflow infer it.
UC uses three-level names. A two-level name is wrong.

questions.scenario: A RAG chain retrieves from an index built with Databricks-computed embeddings from embedding model A. To save cost, a developer changes the chain to embed user questions with a cheaper model B before calling a self-built similarity query.
questions.stem: What is the most likely result?
options: The index automatically re-embeds documents with model B on the next sync
No change, because AI Search normalizes all vectors to cosine space
Retrieval improves, because model B is newer
Retrieval quality drops sharply, because query and document vectors come from different embedding spaces
questions.explanation: Similarity only makes sense when queries and documents are embedded by the same model. Mixing models compares vectors from different spaces, so nearest neighbours become close to meaningless. The embedding model is a RAG building block that must stay consistent between indexing and querying.
rationales: Indexes do not switch embedding models because a client changed.
AI Search uses L2 distance and does not reconcile different embedding models.
Being newer does not make vectors from different models comparable.
Correct: mismatched embedding spaces break similarity.

sources.title: Create AI Search endpoints and indexes — Databricks docs

questions.stem: A model version prod.genai.support_rag v7 passed evaluation. Production jobs load the model by the Champion alias. What is the recommended way to put v7 into production?
options: Delete versions 1 to 6 so version 7 becomes the latest
Re-register v7 under a new model name with a _prod suffix
Update every job to load version 7 by number
Reassign the Champion alias to version 7
questions.explanation: An alias is a mutable, named reference to one model version. Moving Champion to v7 changes what production loads without editing consumers. Deleting history, hard-coding numbers or duplicating models defeats the purpose of aliases and loses lineage.
rationales: Deleting versions destroys history and rollback options.
Duplicating the model loses lineage and is not needed.
Hard-coded version numbers mean editing code for every release.

RetrievalGroundedness
questions.explanation: Correctness compares the response with ground-truth expectations, which unlabeled production traces do not have. RelevanceToQuery, Safety and RetrievalGroundedness grade a trace without expected answers, so they suit production monitoring.
rationales: Works without ground truth; it checks whether the answer addresses the question.
Works without ground truth; it checks for harmful content.
Correct. Correctness needs expected answers or facts, which production traffic does not have.
Works without ground truth; it checks the answer against the retrieved context.

questions.stem: A team has a set of RAG traces but no labeled expected answers yet. Which built-in judges can they run on these traces right away? (Select two.)
options: RetrievalGroundedness
RetrievalSufficiency
Safety
ToolCallCorrectness
questions.explanation: RetrievalGroundedness and Safety need no ground truth. RetrievalSufficiency and ToolCallCorrectness both compare against expectations, so they need labeled data first.
rationales: Correct. It checks the response against the retrieved context, with no labels needed.
Needs ground truth: it checks whether retrieval contains what the expected answer requires.
Correct. Safety grades the response on its own.
Needs ground truth: it compares tool calls with the expected ones.

questions.scenario: Users report that a policy assistant sometimes states rules that appear in none of the retrieved policy documents. Retrieval looks on-topic.
questions.stem: Which built-in judge most directly measures this problem?
options: RetrievalRelevance
RetrievalGroundedness
RelevanceToQuery
ToolCallEfficiency
questions.explanation: Claims that are not supported by the retrieved context are hallucinations relative to that context, which RetrievalGroundedness measures. Retrieval relevance is already fine, and RelevanceToQuery only checks whether the answer addresses the question.
rationales: Measures whether retrieved chunks are on-topic, which the scenario says they are.
Correct. It checks whether the response is supported by the retrieved context.
An answer can address the question and still invent rules.
Grades how efficiently tools are used, not whether answers are supported.

questions.scenario: A team compares a large and a small foundation model for a RAG app. On the same 200-row evaluation dataset, both score within one point on Correctness and RetrievalGroundedness. Traces show the small model has about half the latency and token cost.
questions.stem: What should the team do?
options: Choose the large model, because larger models generalize better to unseen traffic.
Choose the small model, and keep monitoring quality in production with the same scorers.
Pick the model with the higher public leaderboard rank, since the dataset is small.
Choose the model with the longer context window, because RAG prompts grow over time.
questions.explanation: Model selection should rest on your own evaluation metrics plus latency and cost. When quality is equal on the eval set, the smaller model is the better choice, and production monitoring with the same scorers catches any drift.
rationales: Paying more for no measured quality gain is the anti-pattern evaluation is meant to prevent.
Correct. Equal quality at lower latency and cost favors the smaller model, with monitoring as a safety net.
Public leaderboards do not reflect your data or task.
Context length matters only if prompts actually exceed the limit, which the metrics do not show.

sources.title: Evaluate and monitor GenAI apps — Databricks docs

questions.scenario: An agent handles about a million requests a day. The team registered a custom LLM judge for production monitoring and it scores every trace, so judge cost now exceeds the cost of serving the agent.
questions.stem: Which changes reduce the judge cost while keeping useful monitoring? (Select two.)
options: Lower the scorer's sample_rate in its sampling configuration.
Use filter_string so the scorer only grades the traces of interest.
Replace the judge with Correctness, which is cheaper because it uses labels.
Stop production monitoring and rely only on the offline evaluation done before launch.
questions.explanation: Production monitoring scorers take a sampling configuration and a filter_string, so you can grade a fraction of traffic and only the relevant traces. Correctness needs ground truth that production traffic lacks, and dropping monitoring removes visibility into real behavior.
rationales: Correct. Scoring a sample (for example 5-20%) cuts judge cost in proportion.
Correct. Filtering narrows scoring to the traces that matter.
Correctness needs expected answers, which production traces do not have.
Offline evaluation cannot detect drift or new failure modes on live traffic.

questions.scenario: After deploying a RAG endpoint on Model Serving, the team needs to audit the exact prompts and responses users sent and received, and build a new evaluation dataset from real traffic.
questions.stem: What should they enable?
options: An inference table on the serving endpoint.
Query history on a SQL warehouse.
Verbose driver logging on an all-purpose cluster.
A new version of the model in the Unity Catalog model registry.
questions.explanation: Inference tables log each request and response of a serving endpoint to a Unity Catalog Delta table that can be queried for audits and turned into evaluation data. The other options do not capture serving endpoint payloads.
rationales: Correct. It records request and response payloads plus latency and status in a UC Delta table.
Records SQL queries run on the warehouse, not serving endpoint payloads.
Model Serving runs on serverless compute; cluster logs do not capture its traffic.
Registering a model version records the artifact, not its live traffic.

questions.scenario: An engineer enables an inference table, sends a few test requests and queries the table five minutes later. It is empty. The endpoint returned 200 responses.
questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation?
options: Inference tables only log failed requests.
Logging is asynchronous, and rows can take up to an hour to appear.
The endpoint must be recreated before inference tables take effect.
Inference tables only capture traffic sent with ai_query.
questions.explanation: Inference table delivery is asynchronous and the docs say rows can take up to an hour to appear, so an empty table after five minutes is expected. Inference tables log successful requests, and they do not apply to ai_query at all.
rationales: They log normal traffic; some error responses may actually be missed.
Correct. Delivery is delayed, so wait before concluding anything is broken.
Recreating the endpoint is unnecessary and does not speed up delivery.
The opposite: inference tables do not apply to ai_query calls.

questions.scenario: A nightly job classifies 5 million support tickets with ai_query against a batch-optimized system.ai model. The platform team assumes it is governed exactly like their chat serving endpoint.
questions.stem: Which Unity Gateway controls actually apply to these ai_query calls? (Select two.)
options: Usage tracking
Inference table logging
Budgets
Rate limits
questions.explanation: ai_query calls to system.ai route through Unity Gateway, where usage tracking, budgets and permission checks apply. Guardrails, inference tables, rate limits and fallbacks do not apply to these calls.
rationales: Correct. Usage is tracked for system.ai calls.
The docs say inference tables do not apply to ai_query.
Correct. Budgets apply to system.ai calls.
Rate limits do not apply to ai_query on system.ai.

questions.scenario: Several internal apps share one foundation model endpoint. One team's experimental app occasionally floods it with requests, slowing the others and driving up spend.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate control?
options: Add an instruction to the experimental app's system prompt asking the model to answer briefly.
Configure Unity Gateway rate limits for the endpoint, and a budget to cap spend.
Switch every app to priority pay-per-token so requests are served faster.
Turn on inference tables so the team can see the flood afterwards.
questions.explanation: Rate limits stop one caller from exhausting shared capacity, and budgets cap spend; both are Unity Gateway controls. Prompt changes do not limit request volume, priority tier raises cost, and inference tables only record what happened.
rationales: Shorter answers do not limit how many requests are sent.
Correct. Rate limits and budgets are the governance controls for this problem.
Priority pay-per-token costs more and does not stop the flood.
Logging helps diagnosis but does not prevent the problem.

questions.scenario: Clinical experts must judge whether a medical-coding assistant's answers are correct. They do not write code. The engineers want the experts' verdicts to improve automated evaluation.
questions.stem: Which approach fits best?
options: Collect expert labels on traces with MLflow human feedback, then use them as expected answers and to align the LLM judges.
Give the experts edit access to the agent notebook so they can change the prompt directly.
Email the experts a weekly spreadsheet of responses and keep their notes in a shared drive.
Skip expert review and rely on the Safety judge, since it needs no labels.
questions.explanation: MLflow human feedback lets non-coding experts label traces, and those labels become ground truth for evaluation datasets and alignment data for LLM judges. Spreadsheets lose the link to traces, and Safety does not measure clinical correctness.
rationales: Correct. Expert labels attached to traces feed eval datasets and judge alignment.
Lets experts change code without evaluation and does not capture their judgments as data.
Feedback outside MLflow is not linked to traces and cannot easily drive scorers.
Safety checks harmful content, not domain correctness.

questions.scenario: A tool-calling agent sometimes takes 20 seconds to respond. The inference table shows the high latency_ms values but nothing about where the time goes.
questions.stem: What is the best next step to find the slow component?
options: Inspect MLflow traces for slow requests to see the latency of each retrieval, tool and LLM step.
Move the endpoint to provisioned throughput, which removes agent latency.
Raise max_tokens so the model finishes in fewer calls.
Compare time_to_first_byte_ms across days in the inference table.
questions.explanation: Traces record each intermediate step with its own latency, so they show whether a tool, the retriever or an LLM call is the bottleneck. Inference table columns describe the whole request, and changing the serving mode before diagnosing is guesswork.
rationales: Correct. Span-level latency in traces pinpoints the slow step.
Provisioned throughput affects model serving capacity, not slow tools or retrieval.
Raising max_tokens usually increases latency and does not diagnose anything.
Still an end-to-end metric; it cannot attribute time to individual steps.

questions.scenario: During development a team wrote a Python function decorated with @scorer that checks whether responses include a required disclaimer. They now want it to run on live traffic.
questions.stem: What should they do?
options: Register the scorer for production monitoring and start it with a sampling configuration.
Rewrite it as a SQL alert on the inference table, because custom scorers only run offline.
Wrap it in a custom LLM judge prompt, because only LLM judges can run in production monitoring.
Add it to the agent code so the agent grades its own responses before returning them.
questions.explanation: Production monitoring runs registered scorers on live traces, and custom scorers built with @scorer are supported. Reusing the same scorer offline and online is the intended pattern, so no rewrite into SQL or an LLM judge is needed.
rationales: Correct. Register, then start with a sampling config; @scorer functions are supported.
Custom @scorer functions can run in production monitoring.
Code scorers are allowed; an LLM judge would add cost for a deterministic check.
This adds latency to every request and mixes grading with serving.

questions.scenario: A multi-turn shopping assistant gets good per-response RelevanceToQuery scores, but session analytics show many users abandon conversations after repeating themselves.
questions.stem: Which evaluation change best targets this problem?
options: Add multi-turn session judges such as UserFrustration and KnowledgeRetention.
Add Correctness to each turn using the product catalog as ground truth.
Raise the sample rate of RelevanceToQuery to 100%.
Add ToolCallEfficiency to the single-turn scorers.
questions.explanation: Users repeating themselves points to failures that only show across turns, such as forgetting earlier information. Session-level judges like UserFrustration and KnowledgeRetention grade whole conversations, while per-turn judges cannot see this.
rationales: Correct. Session judges evaluate the whole conversation, where this failure appears.
Per-turn correctness misses context lost between turns.
More samples of a per-turn judge still miss conversation-level failures.
Tool efficiency is not the reported symptom.

questions.scenario: Finance asks for a monthly report of model usage by endpoint so each business unit can be charged for its GenAI consumption.
questions.stem: What is the best data source?
options: Unity Gateway usage data in system tables.
MLflow evaluation run metrics from the last release.
Token counts that the model is instructed to report in each response.
The Unity Catalog model registry version history.
questions.explanation: Unity Gateway records usage in system tables (for legacy endpoints, system.serving.endpoint_usage and served_entities), which is the supported basis for chargeback. Evaluation runs and registry history do not reflect production consumption, and model-reported counts are unreliable.
rationales: Correct. Usage system tables are built for tracking and attributing consumption.
Evaluation runs measure test datasets, not production usage.
Models cannot reliably report their own token usage.
The registry tracks model versions, not traffic.

questions.scenario: A team serves a low-volume internal assistant (a few hundred requests a day, bursty) on reserved provisioned throughput. They also run a large monthly batch summarization job through the same endpoint. Costs are higher than expected.
questions.stem: Which change best reduces cost without hurting quality?
options: Move the assistant to pay-per-token and run the batch job with ai_query on a batch-optimized system.ai model.
Keep provisioned throughput and switch every request to the priority tier.
Move to the largest available model so fewer retries are needed.
Disable tracing and inference tables, since logging is the main cost driver.
questions.explanation: Low, bursty traffic suits pay-per-token, and Databricks recommends batch-optimized system.ai models with ai_query for large batch jobs instead of provisioned throughput. The priority tier and larger models add cost, and removing observability saves little while losing the ability to monitor quality.
rationales: Correct. It matches each workload to its cheapest suitable serving mode.
Priority pay-per-token costs more and is unrelated to the idle capacity problem.
Larger models cost more per token, with no evidence of retries.
Logging is a minor cost here and removing it loses quality signals.
